solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Prison sentence passed quickly — that said, it's a strain

parts.note: BIRD is British slang for a spell in prison (from rhyming slang bird-lime, time)

indicators.note: that said tells the solver the previous word is to be spoken, giving a word with the same sound

parts.note: passed quickly means flew, as time flies

explanation.surface: A quickly served jail term is described as a strain on someone.
explanation.walkthrough: BIRD is British slang for a prison sentence. 'that said' turns FLEW into its sound-alike FLU.
explanation.definitionFit: Avian influenza is one particular strain of the influenza virus.

clue.text: In one Transylvanian starter I tasted blood!

parts.note: taken as written
one is the Roman numeral I

indicators.note: starter says take only the opening letter of the following word

parts.note: taken as written
tasted means ate, past tense of eat

explanation.surface: A vampire in Transylvania boasts of having had a first taste of blood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'blood' looks like a noun in the vampire picture, but here it is a verb: to blood a novice is to give them a first experience.
explanation.definitionFit: To blood someone is to introduce a newcomer to an activity, a synonym for admit or induct.

clue.text: Bring to light rogue is in the red? Not he

indicators.note: rogue as an adjective means wayward, so the letters that follow go astray into a new order
Not he says the letters of the word he are excluded from the mix

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether to expose a scoundrel who is overdrawn, then decides he is not one.
explanation.walkthrough: Take IS IN THE RED, remove H and E, and rearrange what is left ('rogue') to get the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To dig up a buried thing is to bring it to light, an idiomatic synonym.

clue.text: Blame talent — not fulfilled — for production being pitifully bad

indicators.note: a production is something made or staged, so the letters are worked into a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: not fulfilled says the word is left incomplete, its final letter dropped

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone blames unrealised talent for a show that turned out dreadfully.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not fulfilled' cuts TALENT to TALEN; that and BLAME are rearranged ('production') to give the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Lamentable means deplorably poor, so wretchedly or pitifully bad is a fair synonym.

clue.text: Tell tales about aide who customarily rings up at work

definitions.text: who customarily rings up at work

parts.note: to shop someone is British slang for informing on them
an aide is a helper or assistant

explanation.surface: Someone informs on a colleague's helper who habitually phones in from work.
explanation.walkthrough: To SHOP is British slang for to inform on. 'rings up' looks like phoning, but means ringing sales up on a till; 'about' is just a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A shop worker who serves at a till habitually rings up customers' purchases on the register.

clue.text: Sheen appearing in film

definitions.meaning: the soft gloss that old wood or leather acquires
a thin surface layer, such as the green coating on bronze

explanation.walkthrough: 'appearing in' is just a link joining the two senses; 'film' is not a movie.
explanation.definitionFit: A patina is both a surface sheen from age and a thin coating film on metal.

clue.text: Caught playing up outside school

indicators.note: outside says the first word wraps around the other piece

parts.note: a machine playing up is malfunctioning, or faulty
C is the cricket scoring abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: A pupil is caught misbehaving outside the school gates.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outside' puts FAULTY around C.
explanation.definitionFit: A university is divided into faculties, each a school of related departments.

clue.text: A stormy threat in the main

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: a stormy sea is churned up, so the letters of the next word are tossed into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A threat of storms hangs over the open sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stormy' rearranges THREAT into THEART. 'the main' looks like the sea, but the definition is the idiom meaning 'mostly'.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases are idioms meaning fundamentally or essentially, mostly true underneath.

clue.text: League loss for Hearts in enjoyable game

indicators.note: loss of one thing for another means the first is swapped out and the second put in its place

parts.note: enjoyable means pleasant
H is the abbreviation for hearts in card games

explanation.surface: A football league result where Hearts lose in an otherwise entertaining match.
explanation.walkthrough: Hearts is also a Scottish football club, which feeds the league surface. 'loss for' swaps PLEASANT's L for H.
explanation.definitionFit: Game here is wild animals or birds shot for sport, and the pheasant is a classic game bird.

clue.text: Willowy model retreats into fiction

indicators.note: into says one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: a fiction is an untruth, a lie

indicators.note: retreats means goes back, so the name is read backwards

parts.note: Kate Moss is a famous British supermodel

explanation.surface: A slender model withdraws into a world of make-believe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'model' points to a famous name rather than a verb: 'retreats' turns her surname backwards (SSOM), and 'into' places it in a word for an untruth.
explanation.definitionFit: Willowy and lissome both describe a slim, graceful and supple figure.

clue.text: Cook pud and eat it for fitness

indicators.note: to cook something is to alter or prepare it, so the letters are made into something new

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Instructions to make a pudding and eat it to get fit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cook' rearranges PUD and EAT IT. 'and' is just a link, not part of the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: Aptitude means suitability or natural ability, as in fitness for a role.

clue.text: See 5
There are no limits to ignominy — however small

indicators.note: however means in whatever way, so the remaining letters can be arranged any way at all
no limits says the outer letters at each end of the word are removed

explanation.surface: Even a small disgrace is boundless, the clue moralises.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no limits to' strips IGNOMINY to GNOMIN, which 'however' rearranges. 'There are' is just a lead-in.
explanation.definitionFit: Mignon, borrowed from French, means dainty or delicately small, as in filet mignon.

clue.text: Question — the first of many — in sample for employer

indicators.note: in says these pieces go inside the other

parts.note: a taster is a small sample
to question is to ask

indicators.note: the first of says take the opening letter of the next word

explanation.surface: An employer quizzes many people as a trial sample.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sample' looks like part of the definition but is the container; 'in' puts the question word plus the first letter of many inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A taskmaster sets demanding work, so a strict employer or overseer fits.

clue.text: Master unusual measure to insulate central heating pipe

parts.note: M is the abbreviation for master, as in an MA degree

indicators.note: to insulate is to wrap around, so the anagram encloses the abbreviation
unusual says the letters of the next word are found in an odd order

parts.note: taken as written
CH is the estate-agent abbreviation for central heating

explanation.surface: A master plumber takes an odd measurement to lag the central heating pipe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pipe' suggests plumbing, but means a smoker's pipe. 'unusual' rearranges the letters to EERSAUM, and 'to insulate' wraps that around the heating abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: A meerschaum is a tobacco pipe with a bowl carved from the white mineral of that name.

clue.text: Inflamed swelling sun yet to set

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for sun or Sunday

indicators.note: to set is to arrange, so the letters are placed in a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Weather report: the sun has not yet gone down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to set' rearranges YET into TYE.
explanation.definitionFit: A sty or stye is a small inflamed swelling on the edge of the eyelid.

clue.text: Growing red cabbage at last after problem with smell

indicators.note: after says this letter follows the previous piece

parts.note: rub as in there's the rub means a snag or problem

indicators.note: at last says take the final letter of the word

parts.note: a scent is a smell

explanation.surface: Red cabbage finally causes trouble because of its odour.
explanation.definitionFit: Rubescent is a literary word for reddening or blushing, going ruddy.

clue.text: Ample time to unwind with middle missing from 'The Matrix'

indicators.note: to unwind is to undo a coil, so the letters are loosened into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: with its middle missing leaves only the first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: Plenty of time to relax watching the science-fiction film The Matrix, minus its middle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to unwind' rearranges AMPLE and T into TEMPLA; 'with middle missing from' cuts THE to TE.
explanation.definitionFit: A matrix is a mould or pattern from which copies are shaped, as is a template.

clue.text: Over-fifties attending Proms upset with traditional German fare

indicators.note: upset means knocked over, so the letters are tipped into a new arrangement

parts.note: O is the cricket abbreviation for over, and L is the Roman numeral fifty, twice
taken as written

explanation.surface: Older concertgoers at the Proms are put out by the traditional German snacks.
explanation.walkthrough: The Proms are a famous London summer series of classical concerts. 'upset' rearranges O, LL and PROMS together.
explanation.definitionFit: Rollmops are pickled herring fillets rolled around a filling, a traditional German dish.

clue.text: Quaint Rye sat either side of bend in river approaching the sea

indicators.note: either side of says the anagram wraps around the other piece
quaint means oddly unusual, so the letters are arranged strangely

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
a U-bend is a bend shaped like the letter U, so bend gives U

explanation.surface: In picturesque Rye, people sat on both banks of a river bend near the coast.
explanation.walkthrough: Rye is a quaint old town near the English south coast. 'Quaint' rearranges its letters with 'sat' into ESTARY, and 'either side of' sets that around the bend.
explanation.definitionFit: An estuary is the tidal mouth of a river where it meets the sea.

clue.text: Pop star refusing to dance to someone else's tune?

definitions.text: refusing to dance to someone else's tune?
definitions.meaning: unwilling to be bossed around or yield, determined and unbending

explanation.walkthrough: Adam Ant was a British pop star of the early 1980s. The question mark flags the playful idiom.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone unyielding will not bend to another's wishes, which is to be firm and resolute.

clue.text: Some of Cabinet once might have had a fag here?

definitions.text: might have had a fag here

indicators.note: Some of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A former government minister may once have smoked a cigarette here.
explanation.walkthrough: A fag at an English public school was a junior boy who ran errands for a senior. Many Cabinet ministers were schooled at this famous school.
explanation.definitionFit: Junior boys at this English public school once served older pupils, a system called fagging.

clue.text: Load a substantial amount in panniers

parts.note: to saddle someone is to load or burden them
bags of something is British slang for plenty

explanation.surface: Someone packs a large quantity into bicycle panniers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bags of' is British slang for lots.
explanation.definitionFit: Saddlebags are bags hung either side of a saddle, which is what panniers are.

clue.text: Piece of bacon with fat on

parts.note: lard is pig fat
taken as written

explanation.surface: A rasher of bacon with its fat left on.
explanation.definitionFit: A lardon is a small strip or cube of bacon used in cooking.

clue.text: Following aborted coup the French created crowning glory of the Pantheon

indicators.note: Following says the second piece comes after the first
an aborted plan falls apart, so the letters come out in a broken order

parts.note: taken as written
la is the French feminine word for the

explanation.surface: After a failed French coup, a crowning monument in Paris was built.
explanation.walkthrough: 'aborted' rearranges COUP into CUPO.
explanation.definitionFit: The Pantheon in Rome is famously topped by a great dome, its crowning glory.

clue.text: Quality rare rump steak with no end of jus

indicators.note: rare steak is lightly cooked, and here the word says the letters are rearranged
with no says the following letter is left out of the mix

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

indicators.note: end of says take the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: A top-quality rare rump steak served without its sauce.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove S (from 'end of jus', with 'with no') from RUMP STEAK and rearrange the rest ('rare').
explanation.definitionFit: Upmarket is used adjectivally for high-quality goods aimed at wealthier buyers.

clue.text: Issue terms of reference without introduction

indicators.note: without introduction says the opening letter is dropped

parts.note: a remit is a set of terms of reference for a task

explanation.surface: Publish the terms of reference with no preamble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without introduction' drops the R from REMIT.
explanation.definitionFit: To issue something, such as a sound or signal, is to send it out or give it forth.

clue.text: Pyrenean peak bordering Spanish kingdom is something to look up to

indicators.note: bordering says the two pieces sit next to each other
peak says take the top, or first, letter of the word

parts.note: Aragon was a medieval kingdom in north-east Spain

explanation.surface: A Pyrenean summit on the edge of an old Spanish kingdom is admired from below.
explanation.walkthrough: 'peak' looks like the mountain, but takes the first letter of Pyrenean.
explanation.definitionFit: A paragon is a model of excellence whom others admire and look up to.

clue.text: Right men getting condemned about attempt to escape

indicators.note: about says this word goes around the other piece

parts.note: a condemned building is declared unfit for use
OR, other ranks, means ordinary soldiers or men

explanation.surface: Correct prisoners being condemned is about to escape.
explanation.walkthrough: OR, short for other ranks, is the crossword convention for soldiers who are not officers; 'about' wraps the word for condemned around them.
explanation.definitionFit: To make a run for it is the idiom for trying to escape by fleeing.

clue.text: Soak and simmer separate ingredients

indicators.note: ingredients are what a dish is made from, so the answer is made from letters inside these words

explanation.surface: A recipe step: soak, then simmer the ingredients separately.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs across 'simmer separate'; the cooking surface hides it.
explanation.definitionFit: To immerse is to plunge into liquid and drench, a synonym for soak.
